structure.title: I. Institutional Background (retail pharmacy market; prescription opioids and their distribution)
III. Differences in Dispensing between Independent and Chain Pharmacies (direct comparison; change-in-ownership DID)
IV. The OxyContin Reformulation and Dispensing for Nonmedical Demand (conceptual framework; identification and results; top diverting pharmacies)
V. What Explains Independent Pharmacies' Larger Dispensing for Nonmedical Demand (competitive pressure; pharmacy ownership)

observations.statement: States that identification proceeds through two distinct designs: a simple cross-sectional comparison of independent versus chain pharmacies with geographic and time fixed effects, and a separate analysis of pharmacies whose ownership changed from independent to chain.

For the ownership-change design, states that identification requires the pre-conversion coefficient on soon-to-convert independent pharmacies to be statistically indistinguishable from zero, treating an insignificant pre-period estimate as a testable implication of the identifying assumption.
observations.note: Retained after the 2026-09-09 outcome-claim sweep: the sentence states what the identifying assumption implies for the pre-period coefficient, which is a design statement, not a report of how the test came out.

observations.statement: Discusses that two-way fixed effects estimators can be biased under staggered treatment timing combined with heterogeneous treatment effects, cites several recent econometric papers on the point, and adopts an alternative estimator as a check on this specific threat.
observations.locator: Section III, discussion before equation (2); Table 3 columns 5 and 10

observations.statement: Frames the OxyContin reformulation as a quasi-experiment isolating the nonmedical-demand component of dispensing, arguing that because the reformulation left medical benefit and price unchanged, any differential post-reformulation decline for independent relative to chain pharmacies reflects a response to nonmedical rather than medical demand.

States two explicit identifying assumptions behind the reformulation design: that the reformulation is uncorrelated with other concurrent factors affecting opioid dispensing, and that it affects only nonmedical demand and not legitimate medical demand for OxyContin.

Acknowledges that its competition regressions cannot be given a causal interpretation because the count of nearby competitors, as well as pharmacy entry and exit, are potentially endogenous, and frames the competition results as informative about incentives rather than as a causal competition effect.

Distinguishes a within-pharmacy competition specification, which combines a mechanical division-of-prescriptions effect with a possible behavioral compensation effect, from a cross-sectional specification without pharmacy fixed effects, and uses the pre- versus post-reformulation split to try to separate the two effects for independent pharmacies.

Motivates a proxy design for pharmacist ownership by comparing headquarters and branch locations of multistore independent pharmacies identified through an external corporate-ownership database, reasoning that an actively dispensing pharmacist-owner is more likely to work at the headquarters location.

Uses pharmacy-level opioid order data from the DEA's Automation of Reports and Consolidated Orders System covering a multi-year period, obtained through a public release of the dataset originally compiled by a newspaper.

States that the unit of observation is a retail pharmacy by calendar month, with quantities of each controlled opioid delivered converted into a common morphine-equivalent-dose measure so that different opioids are comparable.

Restricts the sample to retail pharmacies and excludes pharmacies integrated into hospitals, clinics, or other health care facilities, noting that this exclusion also removes so-called pill mills that both prescribe and dispense opioids at a single location.

Reports adjusting the raw order data for destroyed and returned shipments and excluding large outliers before treating deliveries as equivalent to dispensing, without giving a numerical threshold for what counts as an outlier in the main text.

Describes linking the opioid order dataset to pharmacy geographic identifiers from the same public source, to zip-code-level population and demographic data from the census, and separately to a commercial corporate database used only for the headquarters-branch subsample.

Defines an ownership change using a rule combining a new DEA registration number, a new buyer name, and a change in pharmacy type at the same geographic location within a short time window, with the choice of window explicitly justified in a footnote.

Reports the number of observations in every regression table, and these counts vary across specifications and subsamples, for example because the reformulation analysis is run on both the full study period and a shorter post-2008 subsample.

Defines the main outcome as monthly pharmacy-level dispensing measured in morphine equivalent doses, reported both for all prescription opioids combined and separately for OxyContin alone as a drug considered especially prone to nonmedical use.

Constructs the ownership-change treatment using two separate time-varying indicators, one for the pre-conversion period and one for the post-conversion period, rather than a single pooled treatment dummy, explicitly to let the pre-period coefficient serve as an identification check.
Defines the reformulation treatment as a post-indicator switching on for all months following market entry of the new OxyContin formulation, interacted with the independent-pharmacy dummy.

Constructs a competition variable as a count of other pharmacies within a chosen radius of each pharmacy, and separately decomposes this count into competition arising from independent pharmacies only and from chain pharmacies only.

Presents its main tables with a column progression that adds geographic and time fixed effects one at a time, so that readers can see how the estimated ownership gap changes as successively finer geographic controls are introduced.

Adopts a consistent table convention of reporting the mean of the outcome variable and the estimated effect expressed as a percentage of that mean beneath every coefficient, in addition to the usual observation count and R-squared.

States in every table's notes that standard errors are clustered at the zip code level and adjusted for within-cluster correlation, using the same clustering choice across the direct-comparison, ownership-change, reformulation, and competition analyses.
Does not describe using sampling or regression weights anywhere in the main-text tables, so all reported regressions appear to be estimated as unweighted panel regressions.

Reports zip-code-level clustering of standard errors in every table's notes but does not give an explicit textual argument in the main text for why zip code, rather than some other geographic or pharmacy-level grouping, is the appropriate clustering level.

Reports a figure plotting average dispensing before and after the ownership-change event, with confidence intervals, letting readers visually assess the flatness of the pre-period trend for pharmacies that later convert to chain ownership.

Reports a time-series figure of average OxyContin dispensing by ownership type spanning several years before and after the reformulation, used to argue that pre-reformulation trends for independent and chain pharmacies are roughly parallel, especially in the years closest to the event.

Reports a separate figure showing dispensing trends for all opioids other than OxyContin around the reformulation date, used as a falsification check that no comparable structural break appears in a drug category the reformulation should not have affected.

Treats the statistical insignificance of the pre-period ownership-change coefficient, reported alongside the main post-period estimate in the same table, as a check on the identifying assumption rather than relying only on the visual figure.

Reports an alternative treatment-effect estimator designed to be robust to negative weighting under staggered adoption alongside the standard two-way fixed effects estimate in the same tables, so readers can compare the two directly rather than relegating the alternative to an appendix.

Points to an online appendix for a formal event-study specification of the ownership-change analysis, described only briefly by footnote in the main text and not reproduced as a figure or table on the pages read.

Lists several alternative specifications relegated to an online appendix for the direct-comparison and ownership-change models, including a per-capita outcome measure, an interacted geography-by-time fixed effect, and a coarser quarterly level of temporal aggregation, summarized by footnote rather than shown in the main tables.

Reports the reformulation regression separately for the full study period and for a shorter subsample beginning partway into the panel, motivated in the text by an observation that the pre-reformulation trend looks more parallel starting from that later year.

Describes robustness checks in an online appendix that drop the state with the highest OxyContin dispensing and drop pharmacies at the top of the dispensing distribution, summarized in the main text as yielding smaller but still negative and significant reformulation estimates.

Reports an appendix comparison of the reformulation's effect on a specific high-strength OxyContin dosage associated with nonmedical use against other dosages, summarized narratively in the main text as showing a larger decline for the dosage more sought after by abusers.

Notes an appendix robustness exercise that redefines independent pharmacies by the number of stores they operate and compares each store-count group separately with chains, reporting in the main text only the qualitative conclusion that pharmacies with several stores behave more like chains than like single-store independents.

Constructs top- and bottom-percentile groups of pharmacies ranked by the change in their OxyContin dispensing around the reformulation and compares their zip-code and county-level characteristics, describing this as a descriptive characterization rather than a formally tested hypothesis.

Splits the competition analysis by the source of nearby competition, separately estimating effects of competition coming from independent pharmacies and from chain pharmacies, to determine which type of rival is driving the estimated compensation response.

Presents the competition analysis and the headquarters-versus-branch comparison as two separate tests of two candidate mechanisms behind independent pharmacies' greater responsiveness to nonmedical demand, rather than as robustness checks on the main estimates.
observations.locator: Section V, introduction to parts A and B

observations.statement: States that it examined several other candidate explanations for the independent-chain gap, including differences in patient-history record-keeping, pricing, and pharmacist training, and reports in the main text only a summary conclusion that these alternatives receive little support, with the detailed analysis placed in an online appendix.

Explicitly labels its competition results as offering insight into incentives rather than as identifying a causal effect of competition, given that it treats the number of nearby competitors as potentially endogenous.

Interprets every reported coefficient in percentage terms relative to the mean of the dependent variable, presenting this normalized magnitude as a standard row in each regression table rather than only in the text discussion.

Combines the ownership-change estimate and the reformulation estimate in a footnote to back out an implied share of the independent-chain dispensing gap attributable to nonmedical demand, presenting this as an illustrative calculation rather than a separately estimated model.

States plainly that neither the pooled nor the source-decomposed competition regressions should be read as identifying a causal effect of competition, because the number of nearby competitors and pharmacy entry and exit are potentially endogenous to unobserved local conditions.

Notes that the corporate-ownership database used to locate headquarters reflects only a recent snapshot in time while the opioid order data cover an earlier historical period, so headquarters could be identified for only a subset of the multistore independent pharmacies of interest.
Acknowledges that its name-and-state matching rule for grouping stores into multistore firms is an imperfect proxy that can both overcount and undercount true multistore ownership structures.

Concedes that the two key assumptions behind the reformulation design, namely that it is unrelated to other concurrent shocks and that it affects only nonmedical demand, cannot be tested directly, and offers only indirect supporting evidence rather than a formal test of either assumption.

Reports coefficients and standard errors in its regression tables without asterisks marking conventional significance thresholds, relying on the reported standard errors themselves for readers to judge precision.

Uses choropleth-style maps to display the geographic distribution of both the top-diverting pharmacies and county-level drug-poisoning death rates, placed side by side to invite a visual comparison between the two spatial patterns.

Opens the empirical analysis with a multi-panel summary statistics table that separately covers market concentration, entries and exits, ownership changes, and dispensing levels, organized by pharmacy ownership type.

Previews the paper's central quantitative findings from each empirical section in narrative form within the introduction itself, before any of the corresponding tables are presented later in the paper.

Organizes its literature positioning into three consecutive contribution paragraphs late in the introduction, each tied to a distinct strand of literature: the supply side of the opioid epidemic, asymmetric competition between large and small firms, and the relationship between competition and unethical or illegal behavior.

Reserves the mechanism section, covering competitive pressure and pharmacist ownership, for after both main empirical designs (the direct comparison and ownership-change analysis, and the reformulation analysis) have been presented and interpreted.

Defers many robustness checks, an event-study specification, quantile analyses, and several alternative-definition exercises to a lettered online appendix referenced repeatedly by footnote throughout the main text rather than reproduced within it.

Lists a formal replication-data citation with a persistent identifier in the reference list, following the journal's data-and-code archive convention, distinct from the ordinary literature citations around it.
observations.locator: References, Janssen and Zhang 2023 replication-data entry

observations.statement: Describes its primary dataset as administrative regulatory data collected by a federal drug-enforcement agency and thanks a newspaper for making a processed version of that data publicly available, distinguishing the underlying administrative source from the public access channel used to obtain it.

Identifies the corporate-ownership database used to locate pharmacy headquarters as a commercial private-company database rather than a publicly available source, and describes its general coverage and stated limitations.

Frames the reformulation analysis around a single historical product reformulation event, without discussing whether the estimated response would generalize to other abuse-deterrent reformulations or to a different regulatory or market period.

concordance.paper_says: Reports the ownership-change difference-in-differences model (equation 2) with separate pre- and post-conversion indicators and a chain-pharmacy dummy, estimated with year-month and zip-code (or facility) fixed effects and zip-code-clustered standard errors (Table 3).
concordance.card_shows: Design d1, specs s1 and s2 (Table3.R) run an OLS model of dispensing on Before/After/Chain indicators with zip-code and year-month fixed effects and zip-code clustering, matching the paper's pre/post structure.

concordance.paper_says: States that its preferred ownership-change specification (Table 3 column 4) uses facility fixed effects rather than zip-code fixed effects, arguing this better isolates the ownership-change variation.
concordance.card_shows: Both captured specs for design d1 (s1, s2) use zip-code fixed effects (BUYER_ZIP) together with year-month fixed effects; no captured spec records facility-level fixed effects for design d1.
concordance.note: The card's file-read budget (11 files) may not have reached the facility-FE column of Table3.R; absence in the card does not establish the code lacks it.

concordance.paper_says: Reports the OxyContin reformulation difference-in-differences model (equation 3), interacting an independent-pharmacy indicator with a post-reformulation indicator, in specifications both without and with pharmacy fixed effects (Table 4).
concordance.card_shows: Spec s5 (Table4.do, no fixed effects) and spec s4 (Table4.do, absorb id and Date), both under design d2, regress dispensing on the post-independent interaction with zip-code clustering, matching the paper's no-FE and pharmacy-FE columns.

concordance.paper_says: States in every table's notes, including both the ownership-change and reformulation tables, that standard errors are clustered at the zip code level.
concordance.card_shows: s1 and s2 (design d1) cluster on BUYER_ZIP; s4 and s5 (design d2) cluster on zip; both match the paper's stated zip-code clustering.

concordance.paper_says: Reports the reformulation regression twice, once on the full study period and once on a shorter subsample starting partway through the panel, explicitly motivated by a visual assessment of when pre-reformulation trends look most parallel (Table 4, columns 5-8).
concordance.card_shows: Specs s4 and s5 are recorded without a distinguishing sample-restriction field; the card's automated robustness check flags only an unresolved alt_sample relation between them rather than identifying the subsample columns as a separate pair of specs.

concordance.paper_says: Presents its ownership-change results separately for all opioids and for OxyContin specifically as the two outcome panels of the same table, using the same fixed effects and clustering for both, not as an alternative-fixed-effects robustness check.
concordance.card_shows: The card's automated robustness rule labels s1 (all-opioids outcome) and s2 (OxyContin outcome) as an alt_fixed_effects pair (base=s1, var=s2), apparently triggered by the two fixed-effects terms appearing in a different order in the two formula strings rather than by an actual difference in the fixed effects used.
concordance.note: The two specs use the same fixed effect set (zip code and year-month); the order difference in the R formula string appears incidental, not a deliberate robustness variant.

concordance.paper_says: Presents the no-fixed-effects and pharmacy-fixed-effects reformulation regressions as sequential columns of the same table showing how the estimate changes as fixed effects are added, both estimated by ordinary least squares, not as a comparison of two different estimator families.
concordance.card_shows: The card's automated robustness rule labels s5 (no fixed effects, Stata reg) and s4 (pharmacy and year-month fixed effects, Stata reghdfe) as an alt_estimator pair (base=s5, var=s4), apparently triggered by the different Stata command name rather than a genuine change in estimator.
concordance.note: reg and reghdfe both estimate OLS; the paper does not describe this pair as an alternative estimator, unlike the explicit alternative treatment-effect estimator it uses elsewhere.

concordance.paper_says: Refers by footnote to an event-study version of the ownership-change analysis, stating only that it is shown in an online appendix, without describing its specification or findings in the main text.
concordance.card_shows: A separate spec s3 (design d1, FigureE1E2E3E4.do) implements an event-study regression with leading and lagging event-time dummies and zip-code clustering, but the card's own diagnostic detection records the pre-trend test and pre-trend plot as not confidently found (x1 not_found_in_scope, x2 unknown).
concordance.note: Code implementing an event study exists and is captured as a spec, but neither the paper's main text nor the card's diagnostic tags confirm how its results are reported.

concordance.paper_says: Defines a distinct headquarters-versus-branch comparison group among multistore independent pharmacies with headquarters identified in a commercial ownership database, used as a proxy test for pharmacist-ownership incentives (Tables 7 and 8, Figure 7).
concordance.card_shows: No design or spec record in the recipe card corresponds to a headquarters-versus-branch comparison; the card's two captured designs (d1, d2) cover only the ownership-change and reformulation analyses.

concordance.paper_says: Presents eight numbered regression or descriptive tables and seven numbered figures within the main text alone, not counting further tables and figures placed in the online appendix.
concordance.card_shows: The card's summary line reports only two tables and one figure among its captured outputs, reflecting that only two of the paper's underlying scripts (Table3.R, Table4.do) and one figure script were within the card's reading scope.
concordance.note: The gap reflects the card's limited file-read budget (11 files) rather than a genuine disagreement about what the paper reports.

gaps: No preregistration, IRB approval, or human-subjects consent statement appears anywhere in the main text; the study uses secondary administrative and commercial data rather than newly collected primary data from human subjects.

No explicit textual justification is given in the main text for the choice of zip-code-level clustering over some other geographic or pharmacy-level grouping, beyond stating the choice in every table's notes.

No formal joint statistical test of pre-trends (for example an F-test on a set of leads) is reported in the main text; the only pre-trend evidence shown is the sign and insignificance of a single pre-period point estimate together with the raw trend figures.

The event-study specification for the ownership-change design is referenced only by a single footnote pointing to an online appendix and is not shown or discussed as a figure or table in the pages read.

The lettered online appendix (Appendices A through H, containing most robustness checks, the event study, quantile analyses, and the ruled-out mechanism analysis) is not part of the extracted text and could not be read directly.
No discussion of sampling or regression weights appears anywhere in the main text; all reported regressions appear to be unweighted.

reading.note: Read all 33 pages of the extracted main text in full, including the abstract, introduction, institutional background, data section, both main identification sections (direct comparison and ownership-change DID; OxyContin reformulation DID), the mechanisms section (competitive pressure; pharmacist ownership), the conclusion, and the reference list (which includes the replication-data citation). The lettered online appendix (Appendices A-H) referenced repeatedly by footnote is hosted separately from this extracted text and was not read; its contents are recorded only as pointers in the observations and gaps.
